# Battle of Toychubek

The Battle of Toychubek, also sometimes called the Siege of Toychubek, was a military engagement fought in 1864 between the Russian Empire and the Kokand Khanate during the early stages of the Russo-Kokand War. The engagement ended with Russian forces under General Mikhail Chernyayev capturing the Kokandi frontier fortress of Toychubek.
The battle formed part of a wider Russian effort to break through the chain of defensive positions maintained by the Kokand Khanate across the region. Although relatively small in scale, it contributed to a steady series of advances that eventually led to the capture of Tashkent in 1865.
More broadly, the engagement illustrates how Russian forces conducted their campaign in Central Asia—advancing methodically from one fortified position to the next, and relying heavily on artillery to overcome traditional defenses.
Background
By the early 1860s, the Russian Empire had intensified its expansion into Central Asia. This push was driven by a mix of strategic concerns, including securing the southern frontier and extending Russian influence in the region.
At the same time, the Kokand Khanate maintained a network of forts along the Syr Darya and surrounding areas. These positions were intended to block Russian advances and protect access to the interior of the khanate.
In 1864, Russian forces began systematically targeting these strongpoints, capturing key locations such as Turkestan and Aulie-Ata.
The exact location of Toychubek remains a subject of debate. Some historians link it to a Kokandi fort near modern Kaskelen in southeastern Kazakhstan, though this conclusion is not universally accepted.
Prelude
Following earlier successes, General Mikhail Chernyayev moved against the remaining Kokand positions. Toychubek was one of several forts guarding access into Kokand-controlled territory.
The Russian force consisted mainly of infantry supported by Cossack cavalry and field artillery. In contrast, the Kokand garrison was made up of local troops and had only limited artillery.
Battle
Russian forces laid siege to Toychubek and began bombarding the fortress with artillery. Like many Central Asian fortifications of the time, its mud-brick walls were vulnerable to sustained cannon fire.
Once a breach had been opened, Russian troops launched an assault. Fighting inside the fort was brief but decisive, and the Kokand defense quickly collapsed.
Aftermath
The capture of Toychubek weakened the defensive system of the Kokand Khanate and allowed Russian forces to press further into the region. Continued operations the following year culminated in the fall of Tashkent in 1865.
Significance
Although the battle itself was relatively minor, it reflects the broader pattern of the campaign. Russian forces advanced steadily by reducing the number of fortified positions, while benefiting from superior organization and artillery.
Historiography
The exact identification of Toychubek has been debated by historians. Contemporary accounts, including those by Alexei Kuropatkin, offer only limited geographical detail.
Later scholars have pointed out that differences in spelling and the lack of precise maps make it difficult to match these references to modern locations. Some associate Toychubek with a site near Kaskelen, though this remains uncertain.
As a result, it is still unclear whether the Toychubek mentioned in the 1864 campaign corresponds to that earlier site or to another fort with a similar name.
